clue.text: Chap's giggling — this could make one corpse

parts.note: a chap is a man, so chap's gives man's
giggling is laughter

explanation.surface: A man's fit of giggles is described, with a hint that the laughing might go too far.
explanation.walkthrough: In theatre slang to corpse is to break into laughter on stage, which suits the giggling surface; the definition uses corpse as a noun, a dead body that the crime produces.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlawful killing without premeditation is a crime whose result is a dead body.

clue.text: Fishy lady from Maine — male's captivated by bust

parts.note: ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine

indicators.note: captivated by means held inside, so the male sits within the bust

parts.note: a bust is a police raid
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A woman from Maine catches a man's eye with her figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captivated by' puts M inside RAID; bust is the police sense, not the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A mermaid is a mythical woman with a fish's tail instead of legs.

clue.text: Some deny MP hugged beautiful woman

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A politician denies having embraced an attractive woman.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry and legend a nymph is a lovely young female spirit, so any beautiful young woman.

clue.text: Yellowish green colour under tip of such rock

indicators.note: under places the colour below the tip in this down clue

parts.note: lime is a yellowish-green colour

indicators.note: tip of picks the top letter of the word such

parts.note: a tone is a shade or colour

explanation.surface: A lime shade sits beneath the pointed end of a rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tip of' gives S from such; in a down answer 'under' puts TONE below it.
explanation.definitionFit: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made largely of calcium carbonate.

clue.text: Takes advantage of public transport (not second-class)

indicators.note: second-class grade is B, and not says that letter is dropped

parts.note: buses are public transport

explanation.surface: Someone rides public transport, but only in first class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not second-class' removes B, the second-class grade, from BUSES.
explanation.definitionFit: To use someone is to exploit them, taking advantage of them.

clue.text: Famous ostrich with head in ideal ground

indicators.note: ground means crushed and broken up, so the letters are rearranged
head in picks the first letter of the word ideal

explanation.surface: An ostrich buries its head in the perfect patch of earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head in' gives I from ideal; 'ground' rearranges it with OSTRICH.
explanation.definitionFit: Something historic is important enough to be remembered in history, hence famous.

clue.text: Guarantee Republican dismissed result

indicators.note: dismissed means the Republican is sent away, removed from the word

parts.note: to ensure is to guarantee

explanation.surface: A promise is made that a Republican official's sacking will have consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismissed' takes R out of ENSURE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to follow as a consequence, meaning to result.

clue.text: Recline holding female then get hit — this could keep one up in the main

definitions.text: this could keep one up in the main

indicators.note: holding means the word for recline contains the female

parts.note: to lie is to recline
belt means hit hard

explanation.surface: Someone lounges with a woman, then gets a wallop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts F inside LIE; 'the main' is an old poetic name for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifebelt is a buoyant ring that keeps a person afloat at sea.

clue.text: Private's not to win in court

indicators.note: in places the losing word inside the court

parts.note: not to win is to lose

explanation.surface: A soldier is destined to lose a case in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like a soldier but is the adjective; 'not to win' is a roundabout synonym for a single verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Closet as an adjective means secret or private, as in a closet fan.

clue.text: Recalls politicians after the Queen retires

indicators.note: after places the politicians behind the retreating Queen
retires means the Queen's letters draw back, so they are read backwards

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual abbreviation for the Queen
members of parliament are politicians

explanation.surface: Politicians reminisce once the monarch has gone to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina; 'retires' means it goes backwards, and 'after' says the politicians follow.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall something is to bring it back to memory, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Wife poorly following second drink

indicators.note: following puts the wife and illness after the second

parts.note: poorly means unwell, ill

explanation.surface: A sick wife, shortly after drinking, looks for something more to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts W and ILL after S.
explanation.definitionFit: To swill is to drink greedily or in large gulps, a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Dismayed, a spook has a change of heart

indicators.note: a change of heart here means the central letter of the spook is swapped for another letter, the a in the phrase

parts.note: a spook is a ghost

explanation.surface: A frightened ghost changes its mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has a change of heart' means the middle letter of the spook word is swapped, not that anyone changes their mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast describes someone filled with shock and horror, close in sense to dismayed.

clue.text: Brazilian footballer's blocking bad shot, almost desperate

indicators.note: blocking means the footballer's name sits in the middle of the other letters, obstructing them
bad signals that the letters of shot are messed up
almost means the word shot is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: Pelé is the famous Brazilian footballer, so Pelé's gives PELES

explanation.surface: Pelé gets in the way of a poor attempt at goal and the situation looks hopeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' clips the last letter of shot, 'bad' rearranges what remains as HOS, and 'blocking' puts the footballer's name inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hopeless situation is one without hope, which is what desperate also describes.

clue.text: One should make you better fudge

definitions.meaning: a physician is the person who makes a patient well

explanation.surface: A sweet treat is offered as something to cheer you up.
explanation.definitionFit: A physician cures patients, while to doctor accounts is to tamper with or falsify them.

clue.text: Cleaner wary about boy

indicators.note: about means the word for wary goes around the boy

parts.note: chary means cautious, wary
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A cleaning woman is suspicious of a young lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the wrapping; a charlady is a British term for a woman paid to clean.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlady, or charwoman, is a woman employed to clean houses or offices.

clue.text: Most basic work misspelt

indicators.note: work here is a command to work the letters over, rearranging them

explanation.surface: An elementary piece of work is full of spelling mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' rearranges MISSPELT.
explanation.definitionFit: Simplest is the superlative of simple, meaning the most elementary or basic.

clue.text: Lure me with top off? Crude!

indicators.note: off means wrong or bad, so the letters go astray and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at a tempter who wants them to take their top off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges LURE ME and TOP. 'Crude' looks like an exclamation of disgust but is crude oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude is unrefined oil, which is petroleum as it comes out of the ground.

clue.text: Many capsize entering Scottish island base

indicators.note: entering means the capsizing word goes inside the island's name

parts.note: Mull is an island in the Scottish Inner Hebrides
to tip over is to capsize
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: Several boats overturn as they head for a harbour on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entering' signals the insertion; base gives E because e is the base of natural logarithms in mathematics.
explanation.definitionFit: Multiple means numerous, consisting of several parts, so it means many.

clue.text: Relaxing exercises with expert not quite complete

parts.note: PE, physical education, means exercises
an ace is an expert

indicators.note: not quite means the word for complete stops one letter short

parts.note: full means complete

explanation.surface: A gym session with a top trainer is almost entirely calming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' drops the last L from FULL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something peaceful is calm and restful, so it is relaxing.

clue.text: One's scrupulous editor under pressure with a set of books

indicators.note: under puts the editor below pressure in this down clue

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A careful editor is pushed hard while working on a series of volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' puts ED below P in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant is someone excessively concerned with minor details and rules, overly scrupulous.

clue.text: Disturbances on the radio, still

explanation.surface: Interference keeps going on the radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Static is both radio crackle from interference and an adjective meaning motionless.

clue.text: Cold hospital department radiographer's opening with a large key

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital

indicators.note: opening picks out the first letter of radiographer's

explanation.surface: A chilly X-ray unit is opened with a big key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' gives R from radiographer's. 'key' looks like a thing for locks but is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Key and central both mean of chief importance, essential.

clue.text: Dainty from food shop Charlie consumed

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a food shop
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
consumed means ate

explanation.surface: Charlie eats a dainty morsel from the delicatessen.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicate and dainty both describe something fine, small and refined.

clue.text: Liberal or a Conservative's uplifting song of joy

indicators.note: uplifting in a down clue says the pieces are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal; the letters also happen to sit reversed across these words, a coincidence as the clue has no hiding signal
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A politician of either party finds an inspiring anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: The run of letters looks hidden in 'Liberal or a Conservative', but there is no hiding signal: it is L, OR, A, C built from abbreviations, then turned upwards by 'uplifting'.
explanation.definitionFit: A carol is a joyful hymn, especially one sung at Christmas.

clue.text: Mischievous sprite could make you lose your sight, virtually

indicators.note: virtually means nearly all of it, so the phrase drops its last letter

parts.note: to lose your sight is to go blind

explanation.surface: A malicious little creature might blind you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'virtually' removes the final D from GO BLIND.
explanation.definitionFit: A goblin is a small, ugly, mischievous creature of folklore.

clue.text: Drink stout right to the bottom

indicators.note: to the bottom moves the right to the foot of this down answer

parts.note: stout means large, fat

explanation.surface: Someone downs a pint of stout in one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the bottom' moves R to the end of LARGE. 'stout' looks like the dark beer but means fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is a light beer, a common alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Uprising in Africa is alienating continent

indicators.note: Uprising says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow, running across them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A rebellion on one continent is turning people away.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'Uprising' turns AISA, found in 'Africa is alienating', upwards; 'Africa' is a decoy continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the largest of the world's continents.

clue.text: Nobody attending initially — director's lowest point

indicators.note: initially picks out the opening letters of Nobody and attending

parts.note: DIR is an abbreviation for director

explanation.surface: With no audience turning up, the director hits rock bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes N and A from Nobody attending.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the point directly beneath the observer, and figuratively the lowest point of anything.

clue.text: One in coach, perhaps, sees prang round the bend

indicators.note: round the bend means crazy, so the letters go wild and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone on a bus sees a crash on a corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round the bend' rearranges SEES PRANG. 'perhaps' marks a coach as just one example of a vehicle with passengers; a prang is British slang for a minor crash.
explanation.definitionFit: A passenger travels in a vehicle such as a coach without driving it.

clue.text: Tailor felt alarmed clothing one person in navy

indicators.note: clothing means wrapping around, so the reworked letters surround the one
to tailor something is to alter and refashion it, so these letters are reshaped

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A tailor, measuring a customer, becomes nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailor' rearranges FELT ALARMED, and 'clothing' wraps those letters round I.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleet admiral is the highest rank of naval officer in some navies.
